idiom_name: class hierarchy with internal/fileprivate primitives and an overridden entry method (no protected level)
implementation_notes: Swift deliberately has no protected access level: the access-control chapter lists private, fileprivate, internal, public and open, where internal is module-wide and fileprivate file-wide, so a primitive API cannot be scoped to subclasses the way protected does. The practical realizations are to keep the base and its family in one file and mark the primitives fileprivate, or to accept internal and let every type in the module call the primitives, or to put the primitives on a separate internal collaborator the subclass receives. Overriding is also gated: a subclass outside the defining module needs the class and the member to be open, and override plus super do the mechanics (the inheritance chapter). Idiomatic Swift leans on protocol plus composition for stateless behaviour, with protocol extensions supplying the shared operations; the class form is justified when behaviours share stored state and lifecycle, as in view-controller hierarchies where subclasses override a lifecycle method and compose primitives such as addSubview and layout constraints.
pitfalls: Forgetting open: a class or method that is not open cannot be overridden outside the module, so the sandbox silently stops being an extension point for third-party behaviours.

fileprivate primitives are invisible to a subclass in another file, which shows up as a confusing 'no such member' error; the usual fix - switching to internal - exposes the primitives to the whole module.
Swift has no abstract classes, so an unimplemented sandbox method is caught by fatalError or a protocol requirement at run time rather than at compile time.
A designated initialiser chain (required init) forces every behaviour subclass to forward the base's stored state, which is Swift's version of the constructor pass-through problem.
